title: Viscosity and surface tension: drag, drops and capillaries

sources.title: OpenStax: Drag force and terminal speed
OpenStax: Surface tension and capillary action

chapters.title: Viscosity resists relative motion
points: Dynamic viscosity eta has unit Pa s.
For a Newtonian fluid, shear stress is proportional to velocity gradient.
Parallel layers with eta = 0.5 Pa s, A = 0.02 m squared, speed difference 1 m/s over 0.01 m give 1 N.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Our last class used an ideal fluid with negligible viscous losses. Now let's add something real fluids do: resist relative motion between neighbouring layers. That's viscosity. Picture liquid between two parallel plates. The bottom plate stays still and the top slides sideways. For a Newtonian fluid in a simple steady flow, shear stress is viscosity times the velocity gradient. A gradient tells us how rapidly velocity changes as we move across the layers. If the velocity profile is linear, divide the speed difference by the plate separation. Multiply that gradient by viscosity and area to find the shear force magnitude. Try viscosity zero point five pascal seconds, area zero point zero two square metres, speed difference one metre per second, and separation zero point zero one metres. The gradient is one hundred per second. Multiply zero point five by zero point zero two by one hundred: one newton. The liquid resists the top plate's motion, so an external force must keep it moving steadily. Viscosity is measured in pascal seconds. It is different from density, which measures mass per volume. And this linear stress relationship is a model for Newtonian fluids; it isn't a universal rule for every mixture.

chapters.title: Terminal speed balances three forces
chapters.formula: Stokes drag = 6 pi eta r v; terminal speed = 2 r squared (rho(sphere)-rho(fluid)) g/(9 eta)
points: For slow flow around a sphere at very low Reynolds number, use Stokes' law.
At terminal descent: weight = buoyancy + drag.
r = 1 mm, density difference 4500 kg/m cubed, eta = 1 Pa s, g = 10 gives 0.01 m/s.
chapters.script: Drop a small dense sphere into a viscous liquid. At first it accelerates downward. As its speed grows, the upward drag grows too, until the forces balance. Then it keeps moving at terminal speed. Constant speed does not mean zero forces; it means zero net force. Draw three forces: weight downward, and buoyancy and drag upward. For a sphere moving slowly relative to the fluid at very low Reynolds number, Stokes' law gives drag magnitude six pi times viscosity times radius times relative speed. We also assume the sphere is far enough from container walls that their effect is negligible. At terminal descent, weight equals buoyancy plus drag. Substitute the sphere volume, four thirds pi r cubed, into weight and buoyancy. After cancelling common factors, terminal speed becomes two r squared times the density difference times g, divided by nine times viscosity. For radius one millimetre, density difference four thousand five hundred, viscosity one pascal second, and g ten, the result is zero point zero one metres per second. Watch the square on radius. Doubling radius gives four times the terminal speed only if the Stokes regime still applies. A sphere less dense than the liquid tends to rise; use the appropriate directions rather than treating a negative result as a downward speed.

chapters.title: Surface tension counts surfaces
chapters.formula: Single interface: F = gamma l; thin soap film: F = 2 gamma l
points: Surface tension gamma has unit N/m, equivalent to J/m squared.
It acts tangentially to the interface and perpendicular to a boundary line.
For a soap film with gamma = 0.03 N/m and wire length 0.10 m, force is 0.006 N.
chapters.script: Now look at a liquid's surface. Creating extra surface costs energy. Surface tension describes that cost per unit area, and also the tangential force per unit length along a boundary. We use gamma, with units newtons per metre, equivalent to joules per square metre. This is different from viscosity: surface tension concerns an interface, while viscosity concerns relative motion within the fluid. Imagine a thin soap film on a frame with a movable straight wire. The film pulls the wire toward a smaller area. Here's the easy detail to miss: the film has two liquid air surfaces. Each contributes gamma times wire length, so the total force is two gamma l. With gamma zero point zero three newtons per metre and wire length zero point one zero metres, the force is zero point zero zero six newtons. If we pull the wire outward slowly by one centimetre, work is force times distance: sixty microjoules. The total surface area increases by twice the wire length times the displacement. Multiply that area change by gamma, and you get the same energy. Assume gamma stays constant and neglect gravity and other energy changes in this model.

chapters.title: Droplets and soap bubbles have different pressures
chapters.formula: Liquid droplet: pressure excess = 2 gamma/r; thin soap bubble: 4 gamma/r
points: A spherical liquid droplet has one liquid air interface.
A thin soap bubble has inner and outer interfaces.
At gamma = 0.03 N/m and r = 1 mm: droplet 60 Pa, soap bubble 120 Pa.
chapters.script: Why is pressure inside a small droplet higher than outside? Surface tension tends to reduce its area, and an outward pressure difference balances that effect. For a spherical liquid droplet, the pressure excess is two gamma divided by radius. For a thin soap bubble, there are two interfaces, and the pressure excess is four gamma divided by radius. The film is thin enough that the inner and outer radii can be treated as equal, and gamma is the same on both surfaces. A gas bubble inside a liquid has one interface, so don't automatically give it the soap bubble formula. Let's compare a droplet and a thin soap bubble, each with radius one millimetre and the given surface tension zero point zero three newtons per metre. For the droplet, two times zero point zero three divided by zero point zero zero one gives sixty pascals. The soap bubble gives one hundred twenty pascals. These are excess pressures; add the outside pressure if absolute inside pressure is requested. Now halve the radius while keeping gamma fixed. What happens? Both excess pressures double. The key checklist is radius, number of interfaces, and whether the requested pressure is absolute or excess.

chapters.title: Capillary rise: a vertical force balance
points: Measure contact angle through the liquid; r is the tube's inner radius.
gamma = 0.075 N/m, rho = 1000, g = 10, r = 0.5 mm give rise h = 3 cm.
chapters.script: Finally, why can water rise in a narrow glass tube? At the contact line, surface tension has a vertical component. For a wetting liquid, that component supports the raised liquid column. The tube's contact line has circumference two pi r, so the upward force is two pi r times gamma times cosine of the contact angle. The column's weight is density times pi r squared times height times g. Balance them, and the height is two gamma cosine theta divided by density times g times radius. The contact angle is measured through the liquid. In this introductory model, neglect the meniscus volume and use a narrow uniform tube. Let gamma be zero point zero seven five, density one thousand, g ten, inner radius zero point five millimetres, and contact angle zero. Convert radius to zero point zero zero zero five metres. The numerator is zero point one five; the denominator is five. Height is zero point zero three metres, or three centimetres. Halving tube radius doubles the rise. If the contact angle exceeds ninety degrees, cosine is negative and the model predicts a depression. Before finishing, separate viscosity from surface tension, count interfaces, convert radius to metres, and state the force balance. These are foundations; detailed flow resistance and experimental methods need further practice.

quiz.question: A Newtonian fluid between parallel plates has eta = 0.5 Pa s, A = 0.02 m squared, linear speed difference 1 m/s over 0.01 m. Shear force magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: F = eta A delta v/d = 0.5 x 0.02 x 1/0.01 = 1 N.

quiz.question: In the Stokes regime, doubling a sphere's radius with all other quantities fixed changes its terminal descent speed to:
quiz.explanation: Terminal speed is proportional to r squared. The comparison assumes both spheres remain in the Stokes regime.

quiz.question: A thin soap film has gamma = 0.03 N/m and a movable wire of length 0.10 m. Its pull on the wire is:
quiz.explanation: Both film surfaces act: F = 2 gamma l = 2 x 0.03 x 0.10 = 0.006 N.

quiz.question: A thin soap bubble has r = 1 mm and gamma = 0.03 N/m. Its inside pressure exceeds outside pressure by:
quiz.explanation: Two interfaces give delta p = 4 gamma/r = 4 x 0.03/0.001 = 120 Pa.

quiz.question: A capillary has r = 0.5 mm, theta = 0, gamma = 0.075 N/m, rho = 1000 kg/m cubed and g = 10. The predicted rise is:
